At last we removed two-thirds of the contents to make the box lighter. Even then, lifting it out of the hole took some effort. We placed the removed items among the brambles and left the dog to guard them. Jupiter firmly ordered him not to move or make a sound, whatever happened, until we returned. Then we hurried home with the chest. After an exhausting struggle, we reached the hut safely at one in the morning. We were too worn out to do anything more at once. We rested until two and ate supper, then immediately set off for the hills with three strong sacks that happened to be available. Shortly before four, we reached the pit and divided the remaining treasure among us as equally as possible. Leaving the holes open, we started back. We deposited our second golden loads at the hut just as the first faint light of dawn appeared above the eastern treetops.

We were now completely exhausted, but our intense excitement kept us from resting properly. After sleeping uneasily for three or four hours, we all rose as though we had arranged it beforehand and began examining the treasure.

The chest had been filled to the top. We spent the entire day and most of the following night studying its contents. Nothing had been organized; everything was piled together at random. After carefully sorting it all, we discovered that we were even richer than we had first believed. The coins alone were worth a little over four hundred and fifty thousand dollars, according to our best calculations using the available tables of coin values. There was no silver at all. Every coin was gold, and they were old and varied: French, Spanish, and German money, a few English guineas, and some tokens unlike anything we had seen. Several very large, heavy coins were so worn that we could not read their inscriptions. None was American. The jewels were harder to value. There were a hundred and ten diamonds, some exceptionally large and fine, and none small; eighteen brilliantly sparkling rubies; three hundred and ten beautiful emeralds; twenty-one sapphires; and one opal. All the stones had been broken out of their settings and tossed loose into the chest. We found the settings among the other gold. They seemed to have been hammered out of shape, as though to stop anyone from recognizing them.

“I wrapped it in the paper and pushed a piece into its mouth. That’s how I did it.”

“So you think your master really was bitten by the beetle, and that the bite made him ill?”

“I don’t think it. I know it. Why would he dream about gold so much unless the gold bug bit him? I’ve heard about those gold bugs before.”

“But how do you know he dreams of gold?”

“How do I know? Because he talks about it in his sleep. That’s how.”

“Well, Jup, perhaps you’re right. But what good fortune brings you to visit me today?”

“What do you mean, master?”

“Did Mr. Legrand send a message?”

“No, master, I brought this letter.” Jupiter handed me a note, which read:

“My dear ——, why haven’t I seen you for so long? I hope you haven’t foolishly taken offense at some little abruptness of mine. But no, that seems unlikely. Since we last met, I have had much to worry about. There is something I want to tell you, though I hardly know how, or whether I ought to tell you at all.

“I have felt rather unwell for several days. Poor old Jup’s well-meaning care irritates me almost beyond endurance. Would you believe that the other day he got a huge stick ready to punish me? I had slipped away and spent the day alone in the mainland hills. I honestly think only my sickly appearance saved me from a beating.

“I have added nothing to my collection since we met.

“If you can possibly manage it, come back with Jupiter. Please do come. I need to see you tonight about an important matter. I assure you it is of the greatest importance.

“Always yours, William Legrand.”

Something in the letter’s tone deeply disturbed me. Its whole style was unlike Legrand’s usual writing. What could he be imagining? What new obsession had taken hold of his excitable mind? What business of the “greatest importance” could he possibly have? Jupiter’s account was not reassuring. I feared that the constant weight of misfortune had finally damaged my friend’s reason. Without hesitating, I prepared to accompany the Black man.

At the wharf, I noticed a scythe and three spades in the bottom of the boat we were about to board. They all looked new.

“What is all this for, Jup?”

“But,” I said, handing back the slip, “I remain entirely in the dark. If solving this riddle would bring me every jewel of Golconda, I am certain I could not win them.”

“Yet,” Legrand replied, “its solution is far less difficult than a first hurried glance at the symbols might suggest. Anyone could readily surmise that these marks constitute a cipher—that they express a meaning. But from what we know of Kidd, I could not credit him with devising any particularly intricate cryptograph. I decided immediately that this must be a simple example, though one that a sailor’s uncultivated understanding would deem utterly impossible to read without the key.”

“And you actually deciphered it?”

“Easily. I have unravelled others ten thousand times more obscure. Circumstances and a particular turn of mind have drawn me to such puzzles. Indeed, it is doubtful whether human ingenuity can invent a riddle of this sort that human ingenuity, properly applied, cannot solve. Once I had obtained connected, readable characters, I scarcely considered the mere difficulty of discovering their significance.

“In this instance, as in every instance of secret writing, the first question concerns the language employed. The rules of decipherment, especially for simpler codes, depend upon and vary with the character of the language. Usually the solver must try, in an order suggested by probability, every language he knows until he finds the correct one. Here, however, the signature removed that difficulty altogether. The play on ‘Kidd’ can be understood only in English. Without that clue I should have begun with Spanish and French, those being the languages in which a pirate of the Spanish main would most naturally record such a secret. As things stood, I took the cryptograph to be English.

“You will notice that the words are not separated. With spaces, the undertaking would have been relatively easy. I should then have begun by comparing and examining the shorter words. Had a word consisting of one letter appeared—as would most probably happen, with ‘a’ or ‘I,’ for instance—I should have regarded success as certain. Since no such divisions exist, however, I first had to determine which letters occurred most often and which appeared least frequently.
